title: Taylor Swift Releases “Babylon,” Fans Search for Meaning of New Track
seoTitle: Taylor Swift Releases 'Babylon,' Fans Seek Meaning
subtitle: The Song is Part of The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore Deluxe Edition
excerpt: Taylor Swift has released “Babylon,” the sixteenth track from the deluxe edition The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, reigniting interpretations of lost loves and.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Last Friday, Taylor Swift released the deluxe edition “The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore,” which includes four new songs, among them “Babylon.” The track quickly became a topic of discussion on fan networks, who are seeking to understand its historical and narrative references.

“Babylon” and the Continuation of Previous Themes

The song revisits the reference to the ancient city of Babylon and the Hanging Gardens, already mentioned by Swift in “Cowboy Like Me” from the 2020 album Evermore, where she sings “Now you hang from my lips like the Gardens of Babylon.” The new title suggests a development of the story initiated in that song, as fan analyses indicate.

Lyrics Describing a Romance That Ended

The chorus features the line “You hate this song, but you wake up on the train with your headphones gone / Then that melody is all you want,” indicating that the narrator only realizes the value of the relationship after losing it. In verses, the lyrics mention “You’re using nostalgia as a weapon to hurt yourself / But darling, you end up hurting everybody else,” reinforcing the theme of regret and the consequences of past choices.

Narrative Context: Travel, Casino, and Small Towns

According to one source's description, the story partly takes place in a casino and on a train, with references to a small town in Virginia. The character seems to reflect on decisions to leave home, face the casino's “cage,” and at the same time, miss simple things, like “No elbows on the table, and the neighbors lawn always looked better.”

Connections with Other Collaborations

Swift had previously collaborated with Gracie Abrams on “us.” (2024), which also invokes “Babylon” when speaking of lovers who “hang lifetimes on a vine.” This recurrence highlights that the symbol of Babylon serves to represent loves that are difficult to prove or that may be illusory.

Reception and Curiosities About the Track

“Babylon” holds the 16th and final position on the album, coinciding with the track of the same name by singer Lady Gaga, featured on the album Chromatica (2020). While Gaga's version has a 1990s house sound, Swift's brings folk arrangements, soft guitars, and melodies reminiscent of the “Folklore” style.

With information from Just Jared, Bustle, AOL.com.
